about: Each lineage's own name for the ultimate, the standpoint it speaks from, what it denies, and the reconciliation principle (config/principles.md) that relates it to the others. The one-truth reading is an interpretation-layer hypothesis. Each row records the lineage's own objection, and denials are never erased.

first_principle.text: ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti: 'Truth is one; the wise call it by many names.'
first_principle.verse_in_full: They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, and it is the heavenly, fair-winged Garutmant; the One Being the inspired speak of in many ways: they call it Agni, Yama, Mātariśvan (RV 1.164.46).
first_principle.status: The working hypothesis of this ontology, used only in the interpretation layer (ult:the-one). It is not a claim that any single tradition makes about all the others, and several of the traditions below reject it (see each row's tradition_objections).
first_principle.original: indraṃ mitraṃ varuṇam agnim āhur atho divyaḥ sa suparṇo garutmān | ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanty agniṃ yamaṃ mātariśvānam āhuḥ

rows.name_for_the_ultimate: brahman; ātman; sat (being, one without a second); the fourth (turīya)
rows.how_the_text_says_it: Brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite (TU 2.1.1). In the beginning this was being alone, one only, without a second (ChU 6.2.1–2). That is the real, that is the self, that you are (ChU 6.8.7). 'I am brahman' (BAU 1.4.10). This self is brahman, and it has four quarters (MāU 2).
rows.standpoint: absolute, stated together with apophatic statements; seeker-directed teaching dialogues frame both
rows.what_it_denies: That it can be grasped as an object or described. 'Not so, not so' (neti neti, BAU 2.3.6). Words turn back from it together with the mind (TU 2.4.1). The fourth is neither inward- nor outward-knowing, unseen and ungraspable (MāU 7). It is known by the one to whom it is unknown (Kena 2.3). Some say being came from non-being; the Chāndogya denies it (ChU 6.2.1–2).

principle_relating_it.name: Level of truth
principle_relating_it.reason: The Upaniṣad itself marks a level: 'where there is duality, as it were (iva), one sees another' (BAU 4.5.13–15). Plurality is spoken of from one level, the self without duality from another.

rows.tradition_objections: The Upaniṣads do not systematise. They also state difference (two birds on one tree, MuU 3.1.1–2), and an inner controller who is other than what he controls (BAU 3.7.3–23). The Vedānta schools read these texts as identity, as qualified identity, or as eternal difference, and each rejects the others' reading (dsp:tat-tvam-asi, dsp:souls-one-or-distinct; not yet reconciled). The row records the statements without deciding between those readings.

rows.name_for_the_ultimate: advaya / advaita (non-duality), 'from the standpoint of the highest truth' (paramārthataḥ); the fourth (turīya) of MāU 7
rows.how_the_text_says_it: If the world of plurality (prapañca) existed, it would surely cease. This duality is mere māyā, and non-duality is the ultimate (GK 1.17). There is no dissolution and no origination, none bound, no striver, no seeker of liberation and none liberated: this is the highest truth (GK 2.32).
rows.standpoint: absolute (explicitly marked as the highest truth, paramārthataḥ)
rows.what_it_denies: That duality is ultimately real (GK 1.17). That anything originates or dissolves, and that bondage and liberation are real at the highest level (GK 2.32).

principle_relating_it.name: Level of truth
principle_relating_it.reason: Advaita's own principle: everything plural, the path included, is real at the practical level and sublated at the ultimate level (GK 1.17, 2.32 state the ultimate level explicitly).

rows.tradition_objections: Advaita accepts that truth is one, but it means non-dual consciousness without internal difference. It would reject any one-truth reading that makes the world, plural selves or a personal God ultimately real (ult:advaita-vedanta, caveat). Other lineages object in turn. The Yoga keeps many seers (ot:patanjala-yoga). The Jains keep many souls (ot:jain). The Theravāda denies that the unconditioned is a self (ot:theravada). Śaṅkara's commentaries, which carry the school's full argument, are still skeleton in data/, so this row rests on Gauḍapāda and the Māṇḍūkya alone.

rows.name_for_the_ultimate: puruṣa / draṣṭṛ (the seer); citi-śakti (the power of consciousness); kaivalya (aloneness) as its own state; Īśvara as a special puruṣa
rows.how_the_text_says_it: Then the seer abides in its own form (YS 1.3). The seer is seeing alone; though pure, it looks on cognitions (YS 2.20). Kaivalya is the return to source of the guṇas, empty of purpose for the puruṣa, or the power of consciousness established in its own form (YS 4.34). Īśvara is a special puruṣa untouched by afflictions, actions, their ripening and residues (YS 1.24).
rows.standpoint: analytic (seer and seen); experiential for the path
rows.what_it_denies: That the mind is the seer: the mind is not self-luminous, because it is seen (YS 4.19). That the seen ceases for all when one seer is freed: though it has ceased for one whose purpose is done, it has not ceased, since it is common to others (YS 2.22). Seers are therefore many.

principle_relating_it.name: Standpoint
principle_relating_it.reason: The Yoga speaks of the seer from an analytic standpoint (seer and seen as two), whereas the Upaniṣadic and Advaita rows speak from the absolute standpoint. The shared ground is that the seer is not the mind (YS 2.20, 4.19).

rows.tradition_objections: The Yoga posits many puruṣas (YS 2.22), a real prakṛti, and Īśvara as a distinct special puruṣa (YS 1.24). A one-truth reading would have to treat this plurality as a mere standpoint, and Vyāsa and Vācaspati would reject that (ult:patanjala-yoga, caveat; dsp:one-or-many-purusas). The Theravāda rejects any seer at all (ot:theravada).

rows.name_for_the_ultimate: anādimat paraṃ brahma (the beginningless supreme brahman); Puruṣottama (the highest person, beyond the perishable and the imperishable); kṣetrajña (the knower of the field in all fields); 'Vāsudeva is all'
rows.how_the_text_says_it: The beginningless supreme brahman is to be known, and knowing it one attains the immortal (BhG 13.13). The highest person is another, called the supreme self, the imperishable lord who enters and sustains the three worlds; being beyond the perishable and higher than the imperishable, he is renowned as Puruṣottama (BhG 15.17–18). The one who has knowledge takes refuge in me, knowing 'Vāsudeva is all' (BhG 7.19). The self is unborn and eternal (BhG 2.20).
rows.standpoint: divine (the Lord speaking), with devotional and absolute statements side by side
rows.what_it_denies: That the self is born or dies (BhG 2.20). That what is real can cease to be, or that what is unreal can come to be (BhG 2.16).

principle_relating_it.name: Path by temperament
principle_relating_it.reason: The Gītā's own principle: 'in whatever way people resort to me, in that way I respond to them' (BhG 4.11). Worshippers of the unmanifest imperishable also reach him, though with more difficulty (BhG 12.3–5).

rows.tradition_objections: The Gītā's inclusion is not neutral. Those who worship other deities with faith worship him 'but not according to the rule' (BhG 9.23), and the way of the unmanifest is harder (BhG 12.5). Every Vedānta school reads the Gītā's ultimate in its own way (identity, the Lord as the inner self of selves, or eternal difference) and rejects the others' reading (ult:epic-teaching, caveat; dsp:bhagavad-gita-aksara-purusa). The Buddhist and Jain rows reject a Lord who is the world's source.

rows.name_for_the_ultimate: nibbāna; the unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned (ajāta, abhūta, akata, asaṅkhata)
rows.how_the_text_says_it: The four establishments of mindfulness are the one-way path for the purification of beings and for realising nibbāna (MN 10:2). The cessation of suffering is the complete fading away and cessation of craving, its giving up and release (DN 22:20). There is an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned; were there not, no escape from the born would be known (Ud 8.3).
rows.standpoint: apophatic and experiential; the person is analysed from an analytic standpoint
rows.what_it_denies: That nibbāna, or anything else, is a self. All phenomena are not-self (Dhp 279). In the ultimate sense the truths are void of an experiencer, a doer, one who is extinguished and a goer (Vism XVI). It also denies that nibbāna is mere non-existence (Vism XVI).

principle_relating_it.name: Level of truth
principle_relating_it.reason: The Theravāda's own two levels: 'person' and 'being' are designations, like 'chariot' for assembled parts (Vism XVIII). Only in this sense can its account sit beside the others: they are not read as speaking of the same entity.

rows.tradition_objections: The Theravāda explicitly rejects any identification of nibbāna with Brahman, ātman or a cosmic ground (ult:theravada, caveat; dsp:nibbana-atta-or-anatta, not yet reconciled). This denial stands, and the row does not absorb nibbāna into 'one truth'.

rows.name_for_the_ultimate: śūnyatā (emptiness), the mark of all dharmas (śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa); prajñāpāramitā (the perfection of wisdom) relied upon; its end is nirvāṇa and anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi
rows.how_the_text_says_it: Avalokiteśvara, coursing in the deep perfection of wisdom, saw the five aggregates as empty of own-being (Heart s3). Form is emptiness and emptiness is form (s4). All dharmas have the mark of emptiness: unarisen, unceased, not stained, not free from stain, not deficient, not full (s6). Relying on the perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva's mind is without obscuration, and his end is nirvāṇa (s8).
rows.what_it_denies: Own-being (svabhāva) in the aggregates (s3). Arising and ceasing (s6). In emptiness it denies even the categories of the path: no ignorance and no ending of ignorance, no suffering, origin, cessation or path, no knowledge and no attainment (s7).

principle_relating_it.name: Level of truth
principle_relating_it.reason: The negations are said 'in emptiness' (s6–s7). The practice itself is not abandoned: the bodhisattva still relies on the perfection of wisdom (s8). The sūtra thus speaks from the ultimate level while the conventional path goes on.

rows.tradition_objections: Emptiness is not an entity to be attained ('no knowledge and no attainment', s7). The Prajñāpāramitā would reject reading śūnyatā as a Brahman-like ground or self (ult:mahayana, caveat), and it does not accept that its negations are one name among many for a positive reality.

rows.name_for_the_ultimate: the jīva's own nature (svatattva) fully manifest; mokṣa (release from all karma); the siddha (the perfected)
rows.how_the_text_says_it: The states of the soul, including the destructional (kṣāyika), are the soul's own nature (TS 2.1). Its inherent states are being a soul, capability of liberation and incapability of it (TS 2.7). Because it has passions, the soul takes in matter fit to be karma, and that is bondage (TS 8.2). Liberation is release from all karma, through the absence of the causes of bondage and through shedding (TS 10.2).
rows.standpoint: substance and mode (the soul is permanent as substance, changing as mode); seeker for the path
rows.what_it_denies: That there is one all-pervading self: souls are many and take the size of their bodies (TS 5.16). That what exists is merely permanent or merely momentary: the existent has origination, cessation and persistence (TS 5.30). That anything but karma, taken in because of the passions, binds the soul (TS 8.2).

principle_relating_it.name: Standpoint
principle_relating_it.reason: The Jain tradition's own many-sidedness (anekānta): other views are partial standpoints on a reality of many souls and non-souls, not names for one substance.

rows.tradition_objections: The Jain tradition denies a single all-encompassing reality and a creator. Liberated souls are infinitely many and remain distinct (ult:jainism, caveat). It accepts 'one truth, many names' only as many-sidedness about a plural reality, never as the identity of all souls in one substance.

rows.family: the self-question across the rows: jīva, puruṣa, ātman, anattā
rows.name_for_the_ultimate: (not one name) jīva (TS), puruṣa / draṣṭṛ (YS), ātman = brahman (Upaniṣads, Advaita), and the not-self teaching (Theravāda; Heart Sūtra)
rows.how_the_text_says_it: The Jain soul's own nature includes the destructional states and being a soul (TS 2.1, 2.7), and souls are many (TS 5.16). The seer is seeing alone (YS 2.20), and the seen continues for other seers (YS 2.22). 'That you are' (ChU 6.8.7). All phenomena are not-self (Dhp 279). The aggregates are empty of own-being (Heart s3).
rows.standpoint: each side speaks from its own standpoint; no shared standpoint is established
rows.what_it_denies: Each side denies the others' central claim. The Theravāda denies any self (Dhp 279). The Yoga denies that the mind is the seer (YS 4.19) and keeps seers many (YS 2.22). The Jains keep souls many and body-sized (TS 5.16). Advaita denies that plurality is ultimate (GK 1.17).

principle_relating_it.name: Level of truth
principle_relating_it.reason: Provisional candidate only (see candidate_readings). All sides agree that the body and changing cognitions are not the true self (dsp:is-there-a-self), but they disagree whether anything lies beyond them.

candidate_readings: P1-level: the Buddhist analysis negates a self found among or apart from the aggregates, which Advaita and the Yoga also call not-self. Advaita's witness and the Yoga's seer are said never to be an object of such analysis. The Buddhist logicians refute these selves too, and Advaita asserts the self as being-consciousness, not an absence.

P2-standpoint (the Jains' own synthesis): the soul is permanent as substance and changing as mode, so the permanent-self and momentary-stream theses each state one aspect. Both the self-affirming schools and the Buddhists reject this as combining incompatible claims.
P4-stage: each doctrine of the self is read as the view reached at one level of practice (the inclusivist ranking in dsp:is-there-a-self). The ranked schools do not accept this ranking.

P5-neyartha / P6-upaya: the Buddha's silence to Vacchagotta and MMK 18.6 ('self' and 'no-self' both taught) are read as teaching fitted to the hearer. The self-affirming schools do not accept that their self is merely a teaching device.
rows.tradition_objections: Every party rejects every candidate reading above, as recorded in dsp:is-there-a-self (queued as RQ-U50-01). Until one is accepted on textual grounds, the product must not say or imply that jīva, puruṣa, ātman and not-self are the same, or that they are related as views of one truth.
rows.user_facing_reason: provisional row: not yet reconciled; never shown as a settled correspondence
